div.head: Chapter 21
div.p: The third reason and conjecture by which it is presumed and must be presumed — or rather clearly proved — that such persons cannot have or have had good faith derives from the preceding one; namely, from the very acts and deeds that they themselves perpetrated and committed, all of which were and are evidently against all natural and divine reason and law, and the acts of cruel and brutish men who possess no judgment of reason whatsoever. They were also and were against the human laws and prohibitions; and acts done against the law, even if done through error without believing one is erring, do not excuse, nor are those who commit them in good faith, as was touched upon above.

How could they or can they claim ignorance and any excuse, those who, finding those innocent nations in their peaceful and secure lands and homes, with their wives and children, committing no injury or harm to anyone, fell upon them and put them to the sword, robbed them of what they had, and placed those they seized in the servitude of the tyrannical repartimiento — when that was the least harm they did them? Others, coming out to meet them on the road loaded with chickens and other gifts to receive them, the reward that was many times given to many was to cut them to pieces, feigning and proclaiming that they were coming out for war in order to go quickly to the towns or to the lord who sent them, so as to have occasion to make slaves, and so they did. How can these most wretched men excuse themselves and claim that they had good faith? And still more wretched are the confessors — both secular clergy and regular — who wish to excuse them, God knows for what reasons; who, demanding as tribute from the lords of the Indians, with the gravest threats that they would burn them alive if they did not give them fifty slaves every three months — not having them, as commonly none of them had any —: the natural lord would go through the town, and from the neighbor who had two sons he would take one, and from the one who had three, two, commanding them to say that they were slaves bought and sold, on pain of being burned, as the Spaniards had threatened to burn him. You would have seen the weeping in the town of the mothers and fathers when this was carried out. Then the branding iron was close at hand to mark them as slaves, for another tyrant had it and marked them willingly enough. These people — how can they claim good faith? Were they ignorant of their own acts, that they were most wicked and evil in every ugliness and malice? And a thousand other forms of consummate malice to destroy those peoples they have used throughout all those Indies and in their parts, lacking the authority of the king, for they never had it; rather, they were commanded to do the complete opposite. And even when the kings did give them authority and command, the deeds did not cease to be tyrannical, since all of them were and have been against natural and divine law. Finally, all the evils and the destruction of souls and bodies of such innumerable peoples have been caused by them, and they perpetrated those evils through their own malice and disordered will, subordinating the life and salvation of their neighbors to the craving they have had and have to make themselves rich and to lord it over those peoples. And so, knowingly and by private authority, they broke all the rules and instructions that the kings commanded to be given. And all of them knew this. And if the captains and governors commanded them or gave them license and room to do what they wrongly did, it did not excuse them, because all could see that those captains and governors were the most cruel tyrants, and that from what was robbed and subjugated the greatest and best share fell to them, and in the end all of it, and there was but a single cause for all.

The fourth reason is the most frequent and widespread reputation that exists in the Indies and throughout all Spain, so universal that there is not a peasant from Sayago who does not proclaim it; namely, that none of those who bring money from the Indies, nor those who join with them in marriages, prosper with what they bring, and it dissolves between their hands; and many of those who are most prudent fear to contract kinship or alliance by giving their daughters or female relations to such men. And this reputation began many years ago and grows each day, so that none of those who have destroyed that world with such most grave sins, neither before the judgment of God nor before men, can have any pretext for excusing themselves. And this fourth reason for their bad faith and perverse conscience ought to have been sufficient.

The fifth is that they themselves — the destroyers and robbers of the greater part of the human race — confess it at every turn: some without shame praising and boasting of it as great and notable feats — and such they certainly were, but in evil —; others, in some measure composing themselves and fearing the rigorous judgment of God, seeing themselves so confounded and guilty of the loss of so many souls, convicted by their own consciences, or by the divine law they hear preached, or by natural reason itself.

This sixth, because almost all of them universally recoil from knowing the truth and will not be enlightened or informed about their pernicious errors; rather they defend those errors with all the strength they have, already obstinate in them, and it avails nothing to confound and convict them with their own deeds of demons, as has many times been done by learned and God-fearing men; for they respond with a thousand absurdities, such as this one: "One soul that has been saved through our efforts is worth more than all those we have killed with our own hands." See what a doubt the tyrants declare to us; yet the wretches do not add that Judas was the cause of redeeming the human race, and now glories, wherever he is, in having brought about so great a good. And there is another most grave sin in which they constantly remain: that beyond keeping those peoples tyrannized and being firmly resolved not to release them, they resist as much as they can any favor or good that the king sends through his provisions for the relief of the oppressed Indians. By all of which it appears manifestly that it is not ignorance but consummate malice in which all or most of them remain; and if in some there is any portion of ignorance, this is affected — for they will not know the truth so as to leave off sinning —; and such persons are held to be fully knowing, and as willingly desiring to keep free peoples oppressed and in harmful servitude and to enjoy what has been robbed, according to the laws. And so those of whom we speak are in bad faith and evil conscience, as can be seen from what is treated in the Gloss in L. vitia, Codex, De adquirenda rerum possessione; et de Bartolo, en la Extravagante, Ad reprimendum, in verbo «remunerationem» quasi infini. Et est textus expressus in L. regula, sed facti, ff., De iure et facti ignorantia et ibi in Glossa Magna; and what is noted by the canonists, in the final chapter and in cap. si diligenti, De prescriptionibus.
